title: When Delay Makes You Wrong
author: Admired Leadership
summary: An argument about the timing of dismissal decisions, aimed at leaders who care about the people they may have to fire. The piece concedes that the investigative work — digging in, listening impartially, erring toward the valued team member where redemption is plausible — is right and proper. Its claim is that leaders face two separate decisions, not one: whether the violation mandates dismissal, and how quickly to act once that answer is clear. The move the piece makes is to isolate the second decision and show that it carries its own reputational stakes. Up to the moment the facts support dismissal the leader stands on defensible ground; any delay after that moment, sometimes only hours, puts that ground at risk. The author frames the judgement as retrospective — later observers will ask 'If you knew, why didn't you act?' — so credibility is determined by the decision made at the moment of understanding. The conclusion is blunt: procrastination converts a leader who was right into a leader who is wrong, and the stain cannot be erased.
points: The piece's structural insight is that investigation and action are separately judged, so a leader can conduct a flawless inquiry and still destroy their credibility in the gap that follows it.
Delay is framed as an unforced reputational loss rather than as prudence — the facts do not improve with waiting, but the leader's standing does deteriorate.
The author is careful to preserve the case for second chances: erring toward the valued team member is right up to the point where the lapse is too large to be redeemable.
The retrospective test — how the decision will read to those who learn later what the leader knew and when — is offered as the practical standard for timing.
Once the reputational damage lands, the roles invert: the leader who hesitated is now the one who has to earn back trust.
quotes: Personnel decisions regarding valued team members who severely misstep or violate workplace standards are always complex and often tortuous. Good leaders care deeply about those they lead and this makes the hard choice to potentially end a relationship even more gut-wrenching.
Good leaders who learn about an incident or violation dig in and find out the facts. They listen objectively to all parties and maintain an impartial lens as to what they learn.

On occasion, the indiscretion or lapse in judgment is too big for a second chance. Leaders have an obligation to their many stakeholders to draw a clear line between what is redeemable and what requires dismissal.

At the conclusion of any investigation into what occurred, leaders are faced with two dilemmas. The first is to decide whether the violation mandates dismissal. The second is how quickly to act if termination is the necessary answer.

Because leaders care deeply about the valued team member and also acknowledge the personal conflict created by taking such a hard stance, they often delay making the final decision. Delaying is a big problem.
Up to the moment where the facts now clearly support the need to dismiss the team member, leaders are on safe and righteous ground. Any delay puts that high ground in jeopardy.
Once a leader is reputationally wrong, nothing can erase the stain. Now it is the leader who needs to redeem themselves in the future. Once the decision becomes clear, delay makes leaders groundless.
